readerTitle: Why Pixar's toughest critics had no power to give orders
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Pixar의 Braintrust, Ed Catmull의 기록) + 가상 적용 (소매 매장, 제조 공장)
insight: 솔직한 피드백이 나오려면 피드백하는 사람에게서 결정권을 떼어내야 한다. 문제를 말하는 사람과 고치는 사람을 나누면 솔직함이 덜 위험해진다.
misconception: 윗사람이 직접 검토하고 수정 지시를 내려야 품질이 오른다. '솔직하게 말해 달라'고 부탁하면 사람들이 솔직해진다.

sources.text: Catmull, E. with Wallace, A. (2014). Creativity, Inc. Random House. (Braintrust의 운영 방식, 결정권이 없다는 원칙, 초기 버전이 대부분 좋지 않다는 서술, Toy Story 2 위기)
Catmull, E. (2008). How Pixar Fosters Collective Creativity. Harvard Business Review.
Brave(2012) 감독 교체에 관한 언론 보도 (Brenda Chapman → Mark Andrews)

factChecks.note: Braintrust가 '몇 달마다' 제작 중인 영화를 본다는 표현은 Creativity, Inc.의 서술을 바탕으로 했습니다. 정확한 주기는 영화마다 달라 카드에는 'every few months'로만 적었습니다.
Braintrust의 기원: Catmull은 Toy Story 제작진의 협업에서 시작해 Toy Story 2 위기(제작 후반 대대적 수정) 동안 자리 잡았다고 설명합니다. 원문 표현을 게시 전 다시 확인하세요. Catmull의 유명한 문장('early on, all of our movies suck')은 직접 인용하지 않고 풀어 썼습니다.
'Braintrust는 결정권이 없고 감독이 무엇을 반영할지 정한다'는 원칙은 Creativity, Inc.와 HBR(2008)에 나옵니다. 게시 전 확인하세요.
Pixar가 이야기가 풀리지 않을 때 감독을 교체한 사례(Brave 등)는 언론 보도로 확인되는 내용입니다. 카드에는 구체적 내부 사정 없이 'has replaced directors on some films'로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Why Pixar's toughest critics had no power to give orders
body: Ed Catmull, Pixar's co-founder, wrote that nearly every Pixar film starts out bad. Early versions are confusing, flat or just dull.
The fix wasn't a stricter boss. It was a room of blunt critics who were not allowed to tell the director what to do.

image.label: A small group watching a rough film cut in a screening room
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 시사실에서 5~6명이 거친 스토리보드 화면을 보고 있고, 한 사람만 앞쪽에서 메모장을 들고 듣는 중. 실제 캐릭터, 로고, 영화 장면은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your films are in trouble halfway through.
body: You run an animation studio. Each film has one director and takes years to make. Midway, most of them have serious story problems.
You have several experienced directors on staff. How should they help a film that's stuck?

options.text: Have senior directors review each film and sign off on required changes
options.feedback: You gain control and consistency. But once notes become orders, directors defend their work instead of exposing problems, and reviewers soften what they say.

options.text: Have senior directors give blunt notes, but leave every decision to the film's director
options.feedback: Reviewers can be fully candid because they're not taking over, and the director stays responsible for the fix. The cost is that you must trust the director to act.

options.text: Keep feedback private: only the studio head reviews each film
options.feedback: It's simple and protects the director's pride. But one viewer sees fewer problems, and feedback from the boss always carries the weight of a command.

cards.title: The Braintrust
body: Pixar created a small group of its most experienced filmmakers, called the **Braintrust**. Every few months, it watches a film in progress and says what isn't working.
The group grew out of the core team behind Toy Story. It took shape as Pixar rescued Toy Story 2, a sequel in serious trouble late in production.
The rule that made it work: the Braintrust has no authority. The director decides which notes to use and how.

cards.title: Separate candor from command
body: Honest feedback is risky when the person giving it also holds power over you. You hear a verdict, not a note. So you hide weak spots.

Pixar split the two jobs. Peers **name the problems**. The owner of the work **chooses the fix**. Without the threat of being overruled, directors could hear hard truths, and reviewers could say them plainly.

image.label: Two separated boxes: 'Name the problem' and 'Decide the fix'
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 상자 "Peers: name the problem", 오른쪽 상자 "Owner: decide the fix". 두 상자 사이에 점선 구분선. 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 '메모' 화살표만 가고 '명령' 화살표는 X 표시.

cards.title: A few habits keep the room honest.
body: Catmull described the Braintrust as working only under certain conditions:
list: **Notes are about the work**, never the person
**Reviewers are peers** who have struggled with the same kind of problem
**Problems, not prescriptions:** say what feels wrong, let the owner solve it
**Candor is expected,** and so is listening without defending
cards.callout: The goal isn't agreement. It's seeing the problem clearly.

cards.title: The same split works on a shop floor.
body: Picture a chain of home-goods stores. When the regional manager visits, store managers tidy up and hide what isn't selling.

Now pair store managers to walk each other's stores once a month. They point out confusing displays and slow aisles. Each manager decides what to change in their own store. Problems surface earlier, because nobody's job is on the line in that walk.

image.label: Two store managers walking an aisle with a notepad
image.brief: 매장 통로를 두 명의 점장이 함께 걸으며 진열대를 가리키는 장면. 한 명은 메모, 다른 한 명은 듣는 중. 실제 소매 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: No authority doesn't mean no accountability.
body: Peer feedback only works when people trust each other and respect each other's skill. Bolted onto a culture of blame, it becomes a performance.
Someone still owns the result. Pixar has replaced directors on some films when a story stayed stuck. The Braintrust advises; leadership still decides who leads.
And it's slow and emotionally hard. It suits complex work, not routine choices.
cards.softwareNote: Code reviews and design critiques follow the same logic. They work best when the reviewer flags problems and the author owns the fix, and worst when review turns into a gate run by whoever is most senior.

cards.title: Now it's a packaging plant.
body: You manage a plant with four production lines. Each line has a supervisor. Scrap rates are creeping up, and supervisors rarely admit problems in the monthly review with you.
What change is most likely to bring problems into the open?

options.text: Supervisors visit each other's lines and flag issues; each supervisor decides their own fixes
options.feedback: Peers who know the work spot problems, and nobody fears being overruled. You still track scrap rates, so ownership stays clear.

options.text: You review every line yourself and assign the fixes
options.feedback: You gain speed and control. But supervisors learn to hide issues before you arrive, and the fixes become yours, not theirs.

options.text: Ask supervisors to be more open in your monthly meeting
options.feedback: It signals what you want, but the setup hasn't changed. Admitting a problem to the person who rates you still feels risky.

cards.title: Let peers name the problem. Let the owner choose the fix.
body: Feedback gets honest when it can't be mistaken for an order.
**Try it today:** pick one piece of work your team is stuck on. Invite two peers to say what isn't working, and tell them the owner will decide what to do with their notes.
